Additionally, it incorporates a rigorous regression analysis to formally establish the relationship between input and output, thereby enhancing the model's interpretability. Experimental outcomes across multiple datasets consistently demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed approach over prominent machine learning algorithms and renowned deep learning frameworks such as DeepNet, Bayesian Neural Networks, and Light Gradient Boosting Machine.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRCC) serves as a vital representative body for young researchers within ECFA. Between 2021 and 2022, the committee engaged in various activities such as creating a database of young researchers and organizing an online survey to gather their opinions and concerns. In this article, we will outline the committee's structure, highlight its achievements, and discuss the challenges young researchers face and the committee's plans to address them.

Recent advancements in flat optics research, fueled by dual-metasurface technology, have revived interest in line ripples and their ability to focus light. This feature, initially discovered in 1965, had been largely overlooked until now. This paper delves into the optical properties of line ripples and demonstrates their ability to converge and manipulate both radiating and resonant beams. By setting various parameters, such as phase, amplitude, and line width, optical responses like quasi-circular polarization, two-dimensional vorticity, and quasi-3D focusing can be achieved. Computational models and experimental data confirm the efficacy of this optical design for applications like polarization localization, high-ratio beam scanning, and polarization-based focusing.

A key challenge in preparing human-robot collaborative systems for the widespread use anticipated in the near future is ensuring they can learn effectively in complex, dynamic settings. Current implementations are generally confined to laboratory environments and rely on simplified representations; these are inherently limited and cannot be scaled. To address this issue, we will develop a new cognitive architecture for learning through collaboration between humans and robots. This architecture will learn and represent relevant information from the environment in an integrated and transparent manner, enabling the establishment of a shared understanding among agents through learning. By design, it will be capable of adapting to changing situations and can be easily scaled up in various applications. Furthermore, it will be open-source and compatible with various languages, such as Python and C++, allowing it to be modified and customized by the community. We will showcase its capabilities in a real-world application involving multi-agent learning through simulation, and provide a detailed explanation of its components and learning processes.

A long-standing issue in the study of the median absolute deviation has been addressed, namely the lack of a straightforward, unbiased estimator. The median absolute deviation is a crucial measure of dispersion, widely used in statistical analysis and time series in particular. The classic estimator, although not fully accurate, has been the subject of numerous modifications attempting to improve its precision. The proposed bias-corrected estimator in this study, however, surpasses all previous alternatives in terms of precision. The research also shows that under certain non-stationary conditions, this estimator achieves optimal efficiency, behaving similarly to an efficient unbiased estimator obtained under specific stationary assumptions. The findings are supported by rigorous theoretical proof and comprehensive simulation data.

A key area of natural language processing, relation extraction, is primarily concerned with identifying and classifying connections between entities in a text. The intersection of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction presents opportunities for cross-facilitation. This paper explores ways to integrate knowledge graph link prediction into relation extraction by crossing NLP and machine learning techniques. Specifically, it examines the effectiveness of training a single joint model that can both predict links between entities and classify relationships in a document. This model, built on a shared representation space, allows for the optimization of relation extraction performance through the incorporation of knowledge graph link prediction objectives. The study demonstrates that this joint approach yields better results than a method solely focused on relation extraction alone and achieves comparable outcomes when compared to a method utilizing two separate models for knowledge graph link prediction and relation extraction. The integration of knowledge graph link prediction appears to have a positive impact on difficult relations and improves overall model robustness without compromising performance on easier relations.

In a study on the properties of a Quasi-particle Debye mass in a N-dimensional QCD-like plasma with both temperature and spatial anisotropy considerations, and a finite baryonic chemical potential, the dissociation characteristics of quarkonia were examined. Employing an approximate formula for the Debye screening length, the findings replicated those of existing research in a 3-dimensional environment. Furthermore, calculations involving finite baryonic potential and spatial anisotropy showed that the dissociation characteristics of quarkonia are largely dependent on the Debye screening length and anisotropy parameters. Additionally, when considering both temperature and spatial anisotropy, the N=3, N=2, and N=1 cases were analyzed to determine upper and lower bounds for the dissociation characteristics of quarkonia.

We examined the magnetic arrangements in Tb3RuO7 utilizing neutron-diffraction measurements under both cooling and applied fields. The results showed that regions with ferromagnetic Ru chains experienced an internal magnetic field from neighboring Tb ions that hindered the formation of an equally spaced, 01L-type long-period magnetic arrangement. Instead, an irregular state with evenly distributed 110 and 111 components occurred. When subjected to an external magnetic field, Tb3RuO7 transitioned into an easily detectable long-period magnetic arrangement with a 4L-type pattern and exhibited antiparallel alignment with the external field. Furthermore, Tb3RuO7 displayed an irregular state within the 4L-type pattern when the external magnetic field fell within a specific range.

Machine learning models aim to create aesthetically pleasing and understandable visual representations of their trained models. Currently, there is a disconnect between visually appealing representations and their accuracy in predicting outcomes. For example, even simple image classifiers can generate detailed image representations, but these often lack predictive value. We explore the possibility of creating representations that accurately predict target outcomes, focusing on local visual features that are easily interpretable and versatile across different datasets. We introduce the Modulated Periodic Activation layer (MPA), a flexible neural network component that can capture various feature patterns in image data. The MPA's modular structure allows it to accurately represent both local detailed features and broader contextual elements. We demonstrate that models utilizing the MPA can accurately predict target images or generate synthetic images in specific styles, all while providing a clear visual depiction of the image. Furthermore, our approach is adaptable and can be applied to both training and inference processes.

Machine learning algorithms can learn flexible models to predict continuous outcomes based on complex data with inherent relationships. However, these algorithms struggle when dealing with changes in data distribution or shifts in available covariates that were not present in the training data. We propose a novel approach that uses both causal and effect information to dynamically adjust for covariate variations and ensure generalizability. Our method leverages the properties of semi-parametric efficiency to create an easily interpretable model that makes efficient use of available training data. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through simulations and showcase its practical application in a real-world study examining the effects of air pollution on cardiovascular hospitalizations.

A comprehensive analysis of deep learning is presented through its geometric representation. This involves dissecting neural networks into identifiable components, each corresponding to fundamental mathematical structures. By examining the underlying mathematical framework of deep learning, insights are gained into its operational mechanisms and the interconnectedness of its components. This study explores how individual network units process information and illustrates the inherent complexity of deep learning models, often necessitating sophisticated mathematical tools for interpretation. Although the discussion centers on the most widely used architecture, the principles discussed are adaptable to various other deep learning models.

Lattice minima play a crucial part in determining elastic properties of solids. A comprehensive approach involves examining both primary lattice minima and secondary ones. Primary lattice minima are chosen based on key factors such as acoustic branch division points, the four-fold symmetry of diamond and zinc blende structures, and certain branch splitting rules. A general method to obtain all secondary minima is also proposed, and additional criteria are suggested to verify the stability of these minima. This framework has been successfully applied to silicon and diamond, yielding results consistent with existing research. Furthermore, this approach has practical implications for developing novel phononic materials.

A new technique called Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation (LWRP) is introduced and demonstrated with deep neural networks in a case study of Quantum Chromodynamics simulations. Similar to Varible, LWRP can reveal the decision-making process of a network by tracing the influence of its inputs, but without the need for additional training. In the context of jet substructure analysis, LWRP is used to quantify the contribution of sub-jets within a jet, allowing for accurate recovery of the network's classification capabilities when one sub-jet is removed. This capability is shown to extend to networks with multiple layers and outcomes, as well as networks with separate input quantities, such as momenta and shapes.

For any positive integer n, we define a special kind of Stirling number, denoted by $\bar{r}_n(x)$, which counts the ways to partition a set of n objects into a specific number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains objects separated by a specific distance. When the distance is 1, this formulation aligns with a part of the standard Stirling number of the second kind, often denoted as ${n}{\left[\frac{k}{2}\right]}$. We derive a recursive relationship for these degenerate Stirling numbers and their associated generating functions, which helps us solve related problems, such as finding the total number of partitions where no two objects are in closest proximity. Additionally, we discuss a related concept called the degenerate Stirling number of the first kind, denoted as ${n \brack k}_r$, which counts the ways to place k labeled balls into n unlabeled cells, where each cell has a specified minimum capacity. We establish a relationship between these two concepts through a unique function and then use it to determine the total number of configurations when the distance is 2.

A comprehensive collection of data on irreducible and site-symmetry induced representations for strata groups has been assembled. Specifically, the database covers single, double, ordinary, and gray strata groups. Each entry features essential group properties, along with a tabulation of irreducible and site-symmetry induced representations, all formatted in an easily accessible manner.

A unified momentum operator for a Dirac field is explored in relation to Killing vectors representing geometric symmetry, specifically with scenarios where the manifold's symmetry influences the momentum operator's definition. This study examines cases where integral curves of these Killing vectors act as geodesics. It demonstrates that such momentum operators are singular along Killing horizons and discusses the implications for their use in defining a momentum operator for Dirac fields. Additionally, the paper considers the universal applicability of momentum operators in coordinate systems where Killing vectors are explicitly defined.

A recent breakthrough in quantum chemistry has brought us closer to accurately predicting chemical reactions. However, a persistent problem known as the sign issue has long hindered the development of reliable models. Despite previous attempts to overcome this challenge, the sign issue remains an unsolved problem. In this study, we propose an innovative solution by applying complex-valued neural networks to the quantum chemistry dataset. The results indicate that this approach successfully mitigates the sign issue. The progress made possible by our method enables the creation of highly accurate quantum chemistry models. The techniques we develop and test could be adapted for other complex optimization tasks.

In some composite Higgs theories, where a flavor symmetry is a subgroup of a larger global symmetry, the flavor symmetry model can be incorporated into a fully explicit theory. This is achieved by a Flavon-Higgs scenario, where the Flavon-Higgs Vectors spontaneously break the global symmetry and are parametrically separated from the Higgs boson. A simple, yet comprehensive, effective theory can be formulated through a generalized Yukawa level EFT, capturing all essential properties of the underlying theory. The Flavon-Higgs Vectors' mass dependence in this EFT reveals a distinct correlation, specifically an $E^2$ relationship, which could be substantiated or contradicted by future flavor experiments. Additionally, specific, model-dependent, testable predictions can arise in the underlying theory, relating to Flavon-Higgs Vectors' masses, the flavor-violating Z' boson, and novel, Flavon-Higgs-induced scalar interactions.

Our study examines the effect of visual anomalies on user comfort in Virtual Reality. These anomalies, such as distorted view zones, varying field of view, and aberrant pupil distances, were intentionally induced in our research. Participants were asked to evaluate the level of discomfort they experienced while viewing VR content under both normal and distorted conditions. Our findings reveal that even mild distortions can significantly impair the user's VR experience, leading to increased discomfort. Interestingly, users tend to underestimate the level of distortion based on their head-related transfer function and overestimate it based on eye movement. Our research suggests that VR comfort is largely influenced by perceptual distortions, rather than physical ones.

To assess various approaches to developing universal NLP models, the BigScience project has set language adaptation benchmarks. We investigated adding support for Basque and Scottish Gaelic to a renowned multilingual model, analyzing the impact of several factors on adaptation success, including data quantity, labeling quality, and domain similarity. Our findings indicate that a certain data threshold is required for effective adaptation. Additionally, we demonstrated that fine-tuning with limited high-quality data can yield better results than using larger, more abundant but poorer quality datasets.

Recent high-resolution observations reveal that massive binary systems often have equal-mass stars. Most computational studies have found that equal-mass outcomes result from equal divisions of a parent core, rather than from other mechanisms. To further understand the origins of such systems, we've run a series of computations by expanding a core of 50 solar masses through fragmentation, while varying the total mass of the core and accounting for its rotational velocity. When the core's mass is low (around 20 solar masses), it leads to a system with a primary star much larger than its companion. As the core's mass increases (to 30, 40, and 50 solar masses), its rotation leads to equal-mass binary systems in all scenarios. Masses for the binary components created through this process align well with those from other mechanisms for binary creation, including those proposed by Tohline.

This research presents a novel approach to the Autonomous Component Analysis (ACA) problem,
an unsupervised linear dimensionality reduction technique based on independent component
analysis (ICA). The proposed method, M-ar-K-Fast ACA, offers an optimized and efficient
alternative to existing solutions for reducing large datasets. Its computational complexity
is directly related to the size of the data and automatically adjusts for the dimensions of
parameter matrices, making it suitable for large-scale applications. The algorithm utilizes
an innovative and simplified multi-step training process that expands the traditional
hyperparameter search space, allowing for the automatic estimation of crucial parameters.
As a result, the method performs well in practical scenarios and demonstrates efficient
computational capabilities.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory with algebraic and propositional proof systems. It focuses on two specific theories – Choiceless Polynomial Time and Extended Polynomial Calculus – and explores their capacity to recognize non-isomorphic graphs. By categorizing finite structures according to their manageability by a certain type of formula, researchers have gained insight into the models' limitations and the related proof systems' limitations. This study classifies finite graph properties within this framework and establishes corresponding bounds for the related proof systems. In doing so, it appears that the key barrier to proving a polynomial upper bound for these systems lies not with the existing lower bounds, but with the nature of the underlying structures themselves.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is additive subgroup closed, fully functions over the ring, and includes the ring's zero element, is termed a subring system. Given a ring isomorphism $\phi$ from ring $R$ to ring $S$, any subring system within $R$, when mapped through $\phi$, forms a subring system within $S$, referred to as a $\phi$-subring system. A ring is said to possess the ER (subring extension) property when for each subring system the ring contains, there exists a ring isomorphism $\phi$ to another ring, this time not identical to the first, such that the previously mentioned $\phi$-subring system within the first ring matches the entire subring system within the second ring. A commutative ring with commutative ring homomorphism $\phi$ to another commutative ring, this time not identical to the first, such that the previously mentioned $\phi$-subring system within the first ring matches the entire subring system within the second ring, is said to possess the SER (subring extension) property. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views. While many online comments can be verified or disputed, many more posts are difficult to assess due to their subject matter or lack of supporting evidence. In consequence, a considerable proportion of online discourse is characterized by the presence of unfalsifiable claims - opinions or theories that cannot be substantiated through empirical research and are resistant to evidence-based counterarguments. Despite the challenges posed by such content, many social media users actively engage with unfalsifiable assertions, expressing their views on a range of topics from the nature of consciousness to the existence of supernatural beings. In light of the proliferation of unfalsifiable claims online, researchers are faced with the daunting task of navigating the associated information overload and identifying a framework for differentiating between credible and deceptive content. This paper seeks to investigate the realm of unfalsifiable claims, highlighting existing challenges and opportunities for future research in the realm of online discourse.

Identifying incidents in real-time from large volumes of social media data is crucial 
for swift response and informed decision-making. This process is complicated by the 
presence of noise, such as inaccurate or misleading post information. To resolve 
this, we have developed an approach to accurately detect incidents across various 
locations as they occur, while disregarding erroneous data. This approach employs a 
two-part system that comprises a real-time filtering method using user-specific and 
location-based statistical analysis, and a validation procedure utilizing nearest 
neighbor analysis. To evaluate its effectiveness, we have conducted experiments on 
publicly available datasets related to road incidents in Melbourne, Australia, and 
New York City, USA.

A novel, fast computational technique for examining angular bispectra between Cosmic Microwave Background maps and large-scale structure observations is presented. It's initially applied to the study of CMB data using simulated galaxy count datasets. The method significantly reduces time requirements by avoiding the calculation of two-dimensional convolution surfaces, at the cost of minor accuracy loss. A simplified version of the bispectrum statistic is also introduced, along with a weighted estimation method for reducing noise. The CMB-CMB and matter-matter bispectra are computed using numerical simulations, with a modification to account for the effects of non-linear growth and galaxy clustering. The findings suggest a significant contribution from non-linear processes, particularly at small scales, to the matter bispectrum. The developed methods can efficiently contribute to ongoing research and future bispectrum analyses, such as the CMB-S4 experiment.

By integrating Bayesian learning and adversarial robustness, we develop robust Bayesian estimators on finite metric spaces, satisfying specific conditions. These estimators are based on a novel neural network architecture, which we call the Robust Bayesian Net (RBN), and can be trained on robust data to achieve robust inferences. Theoretical analysis confirms that the RBN's robustness approaches that of an ideal, theoretically robust estimator as the training sample size increases. Experimental results in quantum chemistry and image classification demonstrate the RBN's robustness in various settings and its superior performance compared to baseline methods.

The COVID-19 pandemic originated in China and rapidly disseminated globally, showcasing the rapid spread of online rumors in China, particularly in critical periods. Previous studies primarily focused on the negative impact of rumors, but this research aims to contribute by examining their propagation in China and developing an metric to assess their influence. By collecting Twitter data from January 2020 to February 2020, the authors identified the characteristics of rumors related to the pandemic. A machine learning-based approach and human annotation combined to determine the truthfulness of the rumors collected. Analysis of rumor examples revealed their diverse nature. An algorithm developed to quantify rumor propagation in China identified the nodes involved and the influence of certain rumors. Furthermore, an analysis metric for the impact of rumors was introduced, demonstrating significant correlations with real-world effects in some cases.

This study investigates the effects of applying various spectral dimensionality reduction methods to hyperspectral images, focusing on their implications for pixel classification tasks. A detailed evaluation is conducted by comparing ten methods using multiple indicators and a fully automated, unbiased classification protocol. The analysis considers multiple assessment metrics to gain insights into the interplay between dimensionality reduction and image quality from both a data visualization perspective and a machine learning classification perspective. Our research found that employing a nearest neighbor classifier for hyperspectral images classified with reduced spectral bandwidth yields a substantial reduction in computation time at 10%, however the effect on misclassification errors is minimal. Conversely, using a deep learning classifier showed opposite results, where reducing spectral dimensions led to a notable 30% decrease in computation time but a 10% increase in misclassification errors. Our study demonstrates that various spectral dimensionality reduction techniques yield distinct effects on hyperspectral images, thus recommending against universally applying these methods to such datasets. A particular reduction technique known as Correlated Component Analysis (CCA) stands out as a superior choice due to its capability to maintain low levels of noise in the reduced spectral bandwidths across different evaluation indicators.

Recent advancements in transformer-based language models have led to increased efficiency in text compression. Researchers examining this phenomenon have primarily focused on non-semantic models, whereas those studying semantic models reveal that when trained non-optimally, compressed data can be predicted by model parameters. Our study addresses this by investigating whether datasets can be anticipated from a semantic language model's outputs. The results indicate that, indeed, certain datasets can be guessed before they're seen by the model, suggesting the need for caution when utilizing pre-trained models in resource-constrained environments for text compression purposes.

A novel prediction method for the shifts of protein amide proton chemical shifts has been developed through quantum mechanical calculations. This prediction method is based on empirical patterns identified from the calculations of 35 small molecular fragments. The accuracy of the predicted chemical shifts for a set of 386 proteins is equivalent to a standard deviation of 0.25 ppm, and the method is particularly effective for predicting chemical shifts in difficult-to-interpret regions of the 15N-1H HSQC spectrum. The potential of this prediction method is demonstrated through its application in ensemble models of protein structures, where the method's predictions help to identify and remove non-native conformations. Additionally, the method's effectiveness in evaluating the quality of protein structures is shown in evaluations involving 102 experimental structures and 282 computationally designed ones, and the results indicate that the method can identify up to 70% of the incorrectly predicted structures in ensemble protein models with a high degree of confidence.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a crucial decision that significantly affects the model's performance. The most commonly employed loss function in deep learning is the mean squared error (MSE), yet recent research has demonstrated that other loss functions can yield superior outcomes in image classification tasks. This study aims to investigate how utilizing alternative loss functions impacts the training of deep neural networks and to identify the most effective loss function for a specific task. A comprehensive examination of the influence of loss function on the trained model was conducted, analyzing the optimal models in terms of accuracy, robustness, and generalization capabilities. A comparison of different loss functions revealed that using a modified MSE with hard example mining can lead to a 4% improvement in accuracy, while employing a triplet loss results in the creation of robust models against adversarial attacks. Notably, using the least squares oscillator (LSO) as the loss function yielded models with enhanced generalization capabilities on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis of the LSO loss function provided insights into its behavior and the potential for its widespread adoption in deep learning for classification tasks.

A Hamiltonian-based perspective on the parquet theory is offered, where the parquet graphs are linked to distinct components of a two-particle object. The parquet's utility in computing correlation functions and propagators is highlighted, along with its correlation function's ability to be computed efficiently from a parquet-based Hamiltonian. The choice of a specific parquet and its correlation function is shown to completely determine both the interaction and a one-body potential through a precise formula. This reveals a pivotal connection between a parquet's characteristics and the properties of its associated interaction.

The mechanism behind superconductivity in materials that transition from a non-superconducting to a superconducting state at low temperatures is often attributed to the formation of an exciton condensate. This phenomenon occurs when a group of electrons releases energy and forms a collective state characterized by reduced energy per electron. To fully comprehend the exciton condensate, it is essential to calculate the energy per electron in a precise manner.

We have developed a sophisticated technique to calculate the energy per electron using artificial intelligence algorithms, which can be employed to study exciton condensate in a wide range of materials. This technique involves determining the electronic configuration of a material from first principles and is based on the concept of self-consistency, where the characteristics of one electron are independent of those of other electrons.

To test the effectiveness of this technique, we have applied it to the study of $TiSe_2$, a material known to exhibit exciton condensate at low temperatures. Our calculations reveal that $TiSe_2$ exhibits an exciton condensate, which is in agreement with experimental findings. Furthermore, we have found that our approach enables the simultaneous determination of electronic and phononic properties of a material, thereby providing a deeper understanding of its superconducting properties.

Emergencies can arise at any time and disrupt daily life, prompting individuals to reach out to local dispatch centers and initiate communication. The purpose of these interactions is to convey essential information about incidents, which are often ad-hoc and unscripted. As a result, the language used is spontaneous and unstructured, posing analysis challenges for understanding user intentions and context. To address this issue, researchers analyzed over 668,000 incident reports from Denver's community safety program, applying natural language processing techniques and machine learning frameworks to identify key opportunities for improvement. Their study highlights the significance of enhancing system responses to better support users, particularly by specifying acceptable evidence of involvement and providing clear event outcomes.

In materials with unconventional superconductivity, Cooper pairs can orientate themselves low-symmetry directions. By applying external magnetic fields, s-wave superconductors can transition into the Pauli paramagnetic limit, where the Meissner effect is fully overridden. We investigate how this transition is affected by the orientation of Cooper pairs in nematic superconductors as field direction approaches nematic symmetry axes. Importantly, the compensation of orbital magnetization by Pauli magnetization shows a significant yetthodological orientation-dependent variation, distinct from its isotropic counterpart.

We propose a new framework for simultaneous learning in games, where players' objectives depend on other players' strategies. Our approach maximizes one player's reward while minimizing the other's expected reward in the next game. This framework enables safe policy updates by guaranteeing that the other player's utility function remains within a bounded range. Our method is based on two key concepts: estimating the opponent's reward range and selecting the most beneficial policy when considering the widest possible opposition. To achieve this, we use an adversarial model to update both players' policies, where the opponent's reward range is estimated using self-play. Our system demonstrates better performance than previous methods in multi-player games, including the classic game of poker.

To study how music changed over time from the late 19th century to the early 21st century, we analyzed the melodies of popular songs in the US using information theory. We calculated the informational complexity of these melodies using a measure called Shannon entropy. Our results show that complexity has been decreasing steadily since the late 19th century and predict a continued decline in the future. We also found that complexity varies depending on musical periods and that the most recent songs in our database have the lowest complexity so far. To confirm our findings, we conducted additional analyses and consulted with music experts, which supports our conclusions.

A novel type of stochastic process, called the multiple-entry reinforcement process (MERP), is studied in this paper. An MERP is a specific type of generalized reinforcement process (GRPs), which can also be regarded as a generalization of the Pólya urn model. We investigate key characteristics of MERPs that remain invariant under repeated removals of components and find their asymptotic behavior when the model includes a large number of initial components. An MERP is defined as follows: (i) Start with a set of color-filled objects, where each object contains at least one color; (ii) Remove objects one at a time, and for each object taken out, add a new one, replacing the removed object's colors with those of the original object. Given this sequence of operations, let's examine the final distribution of colors in the objects as the process unfolds infinitely. As it turns out, the final distribution converges to a stationary state, and an explicit formula for the stationary probability of each color $\chi$ is provided: $p_{\chi}=\frac{\sum_{o\in O}k_{o}\prod_{i=1}^{|o|}p_{\chi_i}}{\sum_{o\in O}k_{o}\prod_{i=1}^{|o|}p_{\chi_i}}$, where the sum is taken over all possible color combinations $\chi$ and $k_o$ represents the number of occurrences of each color

We interpret the semantics of a focused proof-calculus known as Computational Ludics. This choice stands out due to Ludics' connection to the semantics of proof and computation, as well as its representation through a system akin to beta-reduction, but with a novel aspect: its control operators derive from the focused structure of proofs themselves, as opposed to standard $\lambda$-calculus.

A key challenge in reward learning is initially not knowing which actions to prioritize without experiencing the environment's consequences. Existing solutions often involve exploring multiple actions in a round-robin manner, but this can be inefficient, especially in a setting with 1000+ actions. To overcome this issue, we've developed an approach that utilizes visual cues to group actions and focus on the most critical subsets. By accurately identifying these subsets, our method allows us to swiftly determine the most valuable actions across various settings, including game maps and robotic arm configurations.

We demonstrate that the Smyth spaces phase spaces are core-compact if and only if they possess a core-compact generator. Consequently, this result offers an alternative proof that the Smyth powerspace is core-compact in the Smyth topology.

We investigate singular vorticity distributions in the form of angular vortex loops within an ideal 2D fluid. These singular objects maintain their configuration over time due to the non-dissipative nature of the fluid. Regardless of initial conditions, they always adhere to a specific point in the fluid. We derive two distinct sets of long-term solutions, each set consisting of multiple vortices. These singularities have significant implications in the long-term behavior of other vorticity distributions in the fluid. Additionally, their presence restricts the applicability of certain theoretical results concerning the fluid's dynamics.

To enhance the accuracy of predictions based on machine learning models, it is crucial to utilize weighting techniques that can effectively mitigate confounding factors. The Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) method is particularly useful in this context. One common limitation of standard IPW is that it may exaggerate standard errors when data points have low predicted probabilities. To address this issue, researchers have developed variations of IPW, incorporating elements from survival analysis to standardize the method. This paper proposes a novel adaptation of the Andersen-Gill IPW method, utilizing neural network predictions and incorporating a variance estimator that accounts for non-convex optimization processes. The proposed approach is demonstrated to outperform traditional standard IPW and alternative weighting methods in a simulation study and two real-world data analyses.

The behavior of taus at their mass-eigenvalue is evaluated in various extensions of the Standard Model, including the Littlest See-Saw Model, Randall-Sundrum models, and a left-right model influenced by electroweak parity. In these theories, which attempt to explain neutrino oscillations, the anomalous tau decays, and the discrepancy in the muon's 1st family decay rate, new particles and interactions are introduced. These extensions often involve the grid-based approach to the renormalization of gauge bosons and fermions in the context of the electroweak gauge boson exchange. The analysis focuses on the modification of the tau's electromagnetic and weak magnetic form factors as well as its electric coupling in the presence of taus to the gamma-Gamma-tau and Z-Z-tau vertices.

A comparative study between experimental and numerical simulations has been conducted to analyze the formation and behavior of baroclinic waves within a rotating, buoyancy-driven fluid in a triangular channel. Both the laboratory test and computer simulation employed the primitive equations to investigate the wave characteristics in this complex system. The experimental study utilized a specially designed facility for studying baroclinic waves and a state-of-the-art imaging system to accurately measure the water surface displacement. In contrast, the computational model utilized a high-performance solver for the primitive equations to accurately replicate the complex processes occurring in the laboratory setup. The test was part of the Diapycnal and Isopycnal Mixing Experiment in the Gulf of Maine (DIMEGM) project, which aimed to understand the formation and behavior of baroclinic waves in the Gulf of Maine. The study found notable discrepancies between the experimental results and computational model outputs, including differences in wave frequency and amplitude. The investigation highlighted potential sources of these discrepancies, including the limited spatial resolution in the laboratory test and the non-equilibrium conditions replicated in the computational model.

A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this approach makes it feasible to use threshold-based data and assess extreme event probabilities, it comes with a limitation: the mean rate of occurrences per unit of extreme event probability cannot be directly estimated. However, this paper demonstrates that combining this strategy with a Bayesian framework allows for accurate estimation of both the mean rate and the parameters of extreme events, using a statistical method that does not rely on specific parameter values. Numerical experiments confirm that this method can provide reliable results even with limited data for small extreme event probabilities.

In the context of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adapting policies to real-world datasets with minimal online adjustment, in the presence of unanticipated deviations from the training data. Building on prior concepts in robust reinforcement learning, we define a corruption-resilient offline policy when nearly all data from a certain Markov Decision Process (MDP) can be learned from a dataset, and this dataset protects a substantial portion of its state-action pairs. We establish the feasibility of finding the most corruption-resilient offline policy in a specified set of policies for a given MDP, and we propose ROAR, an algorithm that approximates this class of policies using a specific type of linear function. Our simulations demonstrate that ROAR is highly effective in a variety of scenarios, and we further analyze the relationship between robustness and the constraints on state-action pairs.

This study demonstrates that for a specific heat equation involving time-dependent source terms and time-varying boundary conditions, the solution's temporal decay is logarithmically concave when accompanied by a uniformly positive boundary function. Furthermore, this research establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for impulsive controllability in a controlled system based on this equation, incorporating an actuator subject to a given reduction capacity and a controller that can instantaneously activate and terminate its action.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We propose a novel approach to uncovering unusual text samples within a language model's domain by identifying negative patterns typically associated with in-domain data. Utilizing a semi-supervised approach, it simultaneously detects out-of-distribution examples and defines their characteristics without the need for explicit labeling. In comparison to existing methods, our solution outperforms in multiple areas, such as accommodating changes in distribution resulting from data transformations and incorporating diverse knowledge sources like Wikipedia. Additionally, it provides clear type-specific detection results, indicating various forms of out-of-distribution data and their relation to detection accuracy.

This study examines the dynamics of Brownian molecular engines powered by inelastic electron tunneling and highlights the distinction between this type of engine, which draws energy from tunneling, and the conventional Brownian motor, which is driven by asymmetry. The investigation focuses on a two-peak tunneling system and shows that this engine can achieve a high efficiency level close to the maximum theoretical value when in comparison to a corresponding Carnot engine. The analysis also considers the effects of fluctuations and non-equilibrium conditions on the engine's performance.

We investigate a non-regular extension of finite state automata, known as word transducers, which process two-dimensional input sequences, and can produce distinct outputs depending on the direction of the input stream. These systems are referred to as directionally consistent if there exists an infinite path throughout the acceptance region, and are considered directionally equivalent if they have equivalent acceptance regions along all possible paths. It's been demonstrated that there is a finite state machine that can model directionally consistent systems, and our study focuses on whether similar models can capture the concept of directionally equivalent systems. Our findings show that this is indeed possible, and we also establish the ability to effectively determine this equivalence relationship.

In this research, we explore the realm of general convolutions, a broad category of operations that encompasses many well-known functions like fast Fourier transforms and polynomial evaluations. We develop efficient algorithms, some of which achieve optimal time complexity, to compute various types of general convolutions. Our findings particularly address convolutions that are commonly AP-parallelizable, like polynomial evaluations and Fourier transforms, and derive new strategies with improved time complexities, such as $n\log n / \log \log n$ for polynomial evaluations of degree $n$, and even reaching the optimal $n\log n$ complexity in certain cases. We also introduce a novel approach, called GAC, for computing convolutions in a parallelized environment, and analyze the computational complexity of several common types of convolutions to find their optimal time complexity.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 was notable, but its age remained unclear.  We have applied the APOLLO retrieval code to analyze spectra of GJ 229B to obtain its mass and age constraints.  We analyzed spectra from three different orbital phases, using a model for its atmospheric composition.  We found a best-fit solution of 37 to 67 Jupiter masses and 1 to 30 million years of age for GJ 229B, assuming it has a mass within this range.  A number of factors could explain the observed spectral features and the age uncertainty.  One possibility is that the planet is accreting material from its parent star, which would require the planet to be closer to its star than the Roche lobe radius.  Another possibility is that the planet is undergoing atmospheric accretion, which would not affect its mass estimate.  Future observations of GJ 229B are required to reduce the current age uncertainty.

Researchers explored the possibility of observing a $0^{--}$ state that contradicts conventional low-energy QED, using data from the BESIII collaboration. A joint BESIII-SND collaboration analysis of the $\rho(1250)$ decay into $\pi^+\pi^-\gamma$ allowed for the investigation of the $0^{--}$ channel's contribution to the $\pi^-\gamma$ invariant mass spectrum. As a control experiment, the study revealed a signal with $5.9\sigma$ significance in the region of interest without correcting for background, yielding an estimated mass $M=(0.838\pm0.018\pm0.035)\mathrm{ GeV}/c^2$. Background simulations indicated the observed signal is potentially a result of $\psi(2S)\to\omega(1250)\gamma$ processes, where $\omega(1250)$ decays into $\pi^0\gamma$ and the $\pi^-\gamma$ invariant mass spectrum exhibits end-point suppression due to kinematic constraints, amounting to a reduction of two orders in signal significance, ultimately resulting in negligible excess events within $2\sigma$ confidence. Consequently, the analysis failed to provide evidence for an exotic $0^{--}$ state.

We have studied the decay process of $b\rightarrow s$ to see how sensitive certain measurements are to how the Standard Model works at specific points. Using simulations of data collected by the LHCb experiment over three years, we observed the decay process of $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ and measured its parameters, including the average lifetime of the $B^0_s$ particle and its decay rate. Our research showed that a certain parameter, known as $\phi_s$, can be accurately measured with high statistics and precision. Although the decay rate of $B^0_s$ can be affected by factors other than the particle's properties, we found that the average lifetime of $B^0_s$ can be accurately measured. Our research also confirmed that a certain complex value, known as $\Delta\Gamma_s$, can be accurately measured.

Airborne viruses can spread through respiratory droplets that have settled or evaporated, often captured by masks, but some transmission may occur from tiny aerosolized particles if inhaled. A recent study simulated virus transport within a confined space, focusing on a simulated urban bus, to determine the effectiveness of masks in a well-mixed air environment. Despite the limitations of this model, our findings revealed that masks can significantly reduce the likelihood of infection when dealing with large droplets, but the protection offered against micro-aerosols is less certain.

This study has undertaken a theoretical examination of the $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray emission associated with the decay of $^{135,137}$Te. Nuclear properties were obtained through large-scale shell-model calculations, incorporating the $np-j$ interaction in a $sd$ space. The results reveal that the emission of 591 keV $\gamma$ rays from $^{137}$I is likely to occur within a brief time frame of 0.2 ns. Conversely, a 706 keV $\gamma$ ray from $^{135}$I is expected to be emitted over a longer period of 1.7 $\mu$s. Furthermore, the study has identified a 280 keV $\gamma$ ray from $^{135}$I as being hindered by an electric nature, exhibiting an unusual electric-to-magnetic mixing ratio. The researchers suggest that the anti-correlation of electron and positron angular distributions at 120 degrees in the prohibited mode of decay could be an indicator of a second hindered transition. The calculated log~$ft$ values for the prohibited modes of decay show significant agreement with experimental data. The study's findings display a satisfactory correspondence with experiments on both the permitted and prohibited modes of decay.

Double-sided auctions are a common price determination method, often used by online marketplaces. Traditional double-sided auctions assume a single buyer and seller, but become infeasible for multiple participants. Our research introduces a new double-sided auction algorithm capable of handling a large number of buyers and sellers. To ensure the auction's validity, we developed a combinatorial auction validation algorithm. Moreover, our method enables simultaneous determination of both buyer and seller clearing prices. Our experimental findings, involving real-world market data from Yahoo!, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

We have systematically computed the mass splittings of F-wave bottom mesons by applying heavy quark effective theory and perturbative QCD at the next-to-leading order. Our findings indicate that the linear mass splittings of F-wave mesons exhibit significant deviations when calculated at the next-to-leading order in comparison to the mass splittings at the leading order. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the linear mass splittings of F-wave bottom mesons are predominantly driven by the lightest scalar and pseudoscalar glueball masses.

In graph theory, periodic divisions refer to a type of partition where the vertices are divided into groups that repeat at regular intervals. Researchers have previously studied the properties of periodic divisions in specific limited graphs. This paper explores how periodic divisions behave in graphs that can be accurately mapped onto a surface with a certain curvature, such as a sphere or a torus, under a specific topology. Additionally, the research investigates how periodic divisions within these graphs are related to paths that do not change direction and may be extended indefinitely.

In systems where analytical solutions are unobtainable, model-reduced methods like Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD are sought after. Our research centers around Kernel DMD (K-DMD), a versatile approach for data-driven spectral analysis. By leveraging a few key assumptions about the underlying system, K-DMD systematically generates an extensive class of model-reduced spectral factorizations. To optimize the methodology and enhance its robustness to noise, we introduce the Kernel Learning for Robust Dynamic Mode Decomposition framework (KL-RDD). This framework utilizes non-convex optimization techniques to develop an overcomplete basis of matrices, effectively generalizing DMD-GA and K-DMD-GA while providing guarantees of spectral and orthogonality approximations. Our findings demonstrate that KL-RDD outperforms DMD-GA and K-DMD-GA in both noisy and noise-free scenarios, with significant improvements in stability and accuracy. Furthermore, KL-RDD exhibits reduced computational complexity and memory requirements. To accelerate optimization, we develop an adaptive learning rate schedule based on the Nesterov accelerated gradient descent method.

This study utilizes a vast chess dataset from the chess website Lichess to examine chess openings in detail. Firstly, the research implements a novel approach to classify moves during games, which are then combined with existing opening classification systems to enrich our understanding. Subsequent analyses involved measuring the complexity of openings by assessing variations within classified groups, as well as comparing them to identify distinct characteristics. Additionally, the research applied statistical methods to group openings based on similarities in game structure, which highlighted notable connections among various openings. Lastly, the investigation explored correlations between player skills and the openings they use, revealing that professional players tend to employ a narrower range of openings compared to non-professionals.

This research explores the potential for advanced neutron stars, also known as millisecond pulsars, to be formed through the process of accretion-induced collapse (AIC) of white dwarfs in binary star systems. Furthermore, this study delves into the operative mechanisms that govern the formation of these neutron stars, particularly the stability of nuclear matter and the response of various probes, and offers explanations for several notable millisecond pulsar phenomena, such as their rapid rotational velocities and commonly found binary connections. The findings of this research support the widely-acknowledged AIC origin of millisecond pulsars and provides new insights to supplement this theory.

A general method for deriving the equations of a Lagrangian has been developed and applied to n-order systems. This application reveals a connection between the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formalisms, facilitating the derivation of a Poisson bracket structure from the Lagrangian coordinates. Building upon this framework, a theoretical model has been constructed to generate dynamical systems, making use of a modified Lagrangian that incorporates arbitrary constraints. This model offers an innovative approach to modeling physical phenomena and exploring the underlying mechanisms, as demonstrated in the analysis of a simple pendulum's dynamics.

This study breaks down 3D shape retrieval into two tasks: first, converting drawings into 3D shapes through spatial layout estimation, and second, matching these estimated layouts to the actual 3D shapes of objects. The primary innovation of this research is an innovative drawing-to-3D approach that learns and generates 3D shapes on its own, in addition to utilizing VR technology for more accurate 3D shape retrievals. The proposed pipeline consists of two main components: a user interface that allows virtual 3D drawing input and a 3D shape retrieval method that compares the virtual drawings' spatial layouts to the 3D shapes of objects. The development of a fully functional 3D drawing interface and a companion web application for gathering user feedback have also been crucial for the research's data collection phase. An extensive user study revealed that the proposed system outperforms existing drawing-based 3D shape retrieval methods and even performs on par with traditional text-based retrieval systems in terms of effectiveness and efficiency.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various atmospheric phenomena. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is essential to plan these observations effectively. Researchers have conducted a new analysis of the planet's transits in 2020 and 2021, updating the most recent estimates from 2019 using a precise model of the planet's size and mass. As a result, they have refined the planet's orbital path to a greater extent than was previously possible using ground-based telescopes. Combining the new data with measurements from space-based telescopes, the researchers have further refined the planet's orbital parameters. Additionally, they have ruled out several alternative orbital models that could explain peculiarities in the planet's transit patterns.

In this investigation, we examine the feasibility of isentropic, spherically symmetric stellar collapses under the influence of a linear equation of state, $p(\rho) = (1-\beta)\rho$. As $\rho$ increases, the adiabatic index becomes negative, resulting in $1/c^2 = 1/(1+\beta)\frac{dp}{d\rho}$. This study demonstrates that such collapses are only feasible if $\beta$ exceeds the critical value $\beta_c \approx 0.294$, derived from inverting the Lane-Emden equation. Failing this, the equation of state would cause the pressure to become too negative, potentially introducing complex behavior and even complex-valued solutions for the metric.

The Iyer-Wald formalism is a widely accepted method for computing corrections to extremal black holes. However, this approach's corrections significantly outweigh the existing corrections from string theory and its variants. In this research, we have discovered that these Iyer-Wald corrections can be seamlessly integrated into the string theory corrections without altering the first eight coefficients, thereby ensuring the correctness of our findings. Our study specifically examines how Iyer-Wald corrections combine with string theory corrections involving four-derivative terms.

The connection between the brain's motor cortex and peripheral muscles has long been examined, yet the underlying mechanisms of motor skill acquisition remain an ongoing area of study. Our objective is to analyze the key factors involved in the development of motor coordination, particularly how sensory feedback from limb movements influences motor learning. We investigate this relationship through a virtual reality experiment where participants learn to move a virtual object via joystick control. By controlling the direction of the virtual object, we can assess the extent to which sensory feedback is necessary for motor coordination and observe the consequences of impaired motor learning. The direction of the virtual object can be set to either follow the joystick movement or an algorithmically generated path. When the virtual object follows the joystick movement, participants experience consistent sensory feedback that matches their movements. In contrast, when the direction of the virtual object is set to an algorithmically generated path, participants encounter unexpected movements that suggest disordered sensory feedback. We found that the majority of participants experienced decreased movement performance along the unintended axis of movement. Our results indicate that the algorithmically generated path created a conflict between motor actions, leading to an increase in movement distance and non-linear movement patterns. Notably, the degree of movement disruption was greater for those with lower hand dexterity, indicating that sensory feedback conflict may have a more significant impact on motor coordination in individuals with pre-existing motor control difficulties. Our study provides novel insights into the role of sensory feedback coordination and suggests that motor learning is driven by an investigation of the causes of movement errors.

The mature development of gauge theories has successfully described various fundamental nature of nature, however the incorporation of diffeomorphism gauge that describes gravity's effect has proven difficult to integrate, especially when attempting to derive actions for particles from a unified theory. Historically, De Donder and Bergra developed a method to isolate vibrational diffeomorphism gauge, which enables the decomposition of gravity's covariant derivative into a flat connection. Subsequent work involved researchers such as Inönü, Sasaki, and Takahashi, who applied this approach to the development of non-relativistic and relativistic particle actions in flat spacetimes. More recently, researchers have expanded upon this framework to include higher-dimensional spacetimes and spacetimes with torsion. This report intends to summarize the key findings from the 1950s to 1960s research and explore its potential applications and developments.

Designing parameterized procedures for graph layout problems is a difficult endeavor. Upward planarity, which involves visualizing a graph in an upward direction without any edge crossings, presents an especially challenging task. In this study, we develop new parameterized algorithms to solve this problem in the following scenarios: (1) when a vertex is fixed and we consider one face as the 'outside' area, (2) for bipartite graphs where we can direct edges from one part to the other, and (3) for graphs with specified orientations of edges. These algorithms have efficient runtime complexities, specifically FPT (fixed parameter tractable), which is better than the FTW (four-tuple-weakly-halting) complexity in this context.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to recall relevant scenes, navigate to those scenes, and then identify them. Multi-task approaches often combine image classification and localization, but typically store all seen images, neglecting their lack of relevance to the navigation task. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of memory management, proposing a novel method, MemoNav, to selectively choose memorable scenes. To accomplish this, MemoNav stores agent-experienced images and learns to predict their usefulness for the navigation task, both based on the agent's forward-looking view and existing goal image. MemoNav outperforms existing methods in various environments, demonstrating the importance of memory management in image-based navigation.

This article provides an in-depth analysis of past, present, and anticipated developments in small cell technology from 4G to 6G. The article initially examines the key aspects and challenges associated with small cell systems in 4G and later in LTE/5G systems. Following this, it delves into emerging technologies such as millimeter wave (mmWave), network slicing, and selforganizing networks (SON), which play crucial roles in future small cell systems. The article also discusses the future of small cell technology in areas like AI-enhanced wireless networks, this piece will focus on the future of small cell technology in 6G systems.

Dynamical systems typically analyze change over time within a singular entity. In contrast, understanding complex real-world phenomena requires considering interactions between multiple interconnected components. This necessity has given birth to the concept of complex systems, which encompass networks of interconnected entities giving rise to emergent collective behavior. This tutorial series delves into the world of complex systems, specifically exploring how dynamics unfold on networks to ultimately shape collective dynamics.

We've developed a unified method to examine the link between operator growth and the representation of a Lie algebra within the context of conformal field theories. Our method views operator growth as an outcome of the increasing complexity of operators when expanded across a basis rooted in the Lie algebra's generators. We derive a crucial formula linking operator dimensions and discuss specific cases involving the $SU(2)$ and $E_8$ algebras in detail. Our analysis of $SU(2)$ reveals a spiral pattern in operator dimensions, consistent with existing research, while exploring $E_8$ presents substantial computational obstacles due to $E_8$'s intricate structure.

A study focused on the radioactive decay of the Hoyle state using the Japanese Gibbs-type Twin Parallelogram Spectrometer was conducted without using intermediate nuclei. Data was collected at 133 energy points spanning 4.52 MeV in sufficient detail to analyze resonances within that range. Research revealed a narrow resonance with 4.4 kilobeves and 0.33 millibeves, along with a previously unobserved state at 13.05 MeV. This new information provides further insight into the Hoyle state's low-energy decay behavior.

The emergence of small-scale irregularities during fracture propagation is a common and long-studied phenomenon in materials. Previous research has identified various factors that may contribute to the development of such instabilities, including the inherent material properties of brittleness, hardness, and work-hardening behavior. To gain a deeper understanding of these mechanisms, we conducted a series of computer simulations modeling two-dimensional dynamic fracture in brittle and semi-brittle materials. The results of these studies reveal the presence of two distinct types of instabilities: an oscillatory behavior that occurs on a small scale and a splitting of the crack tip. The oscillatory phenomenon is primarily influenced by the inherent material length scales, causing the crack to oscillate as it advances as a result of a competition between energy release rate and fracture energy. On the other hand, the splitting of the crack tip is a purely kinetic effect that arises from a complex interplay between inherent material length scales and the dynamic stress singularity. The significance of material length scales in this process is also observed, with an increase in the crack tip splitting angle as the scales become favorably aligned. The findings of these studies offer a new perspective on the factors contributing to the development of small-scale irregularities during fracture, and may provide a basis for a generalized theory applicable across various materials.

We investigate the capacity and optimal power allocation of a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) wireless communication system that employs a finite-state channel model with feedback and knowledge of the channel's state at the encoder. The channel's state is represented as a sequence of random variables that are known to both the transmitter and receiver, while the input and output of the channel are known only at the receiver. Utilizing a finite-state machine representation of this system, we derive the capacity formula and propose an algorithm for calculating power allocation optimization. The proposed approach is applicable to various scenarios, such as correlated channel states and inputs subject to power constraints. We further demonstrate that in the absence of feedback, our power allocation optimization generalizes the well-known vector perturbation approach, while achieving a stronger guaranteed level of mutual information.

A computational model that incorporates the Rashba effect and interactions is used to investigate polarized spin-1 fermions that interact via short-range attractive forces. In a specific region of the phase diagram, at the boundary of a topologically nontrivial area, we demonstrate the presence of a spin-singlet topological superfluid using the Monte Carlo sampling method. We also establish that the spin-singlet component of the superfluid's wave function dominates. Furthermore, we propose that the spin-singlet component is responsible for a spin polarization that arises due to interactions, potentially leading to a spin-symmetric superfluid. We provide a qualitative explanation of the underlying mechanisms within the system, suggesting that the spin-orbit coupling that gives rise to the Rashba effect has a significant impact on the formation of a topological superfluid.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring both validation and evidence-finding capabilities. To test this, we developed a new dataset for a SemEval task and received submissions from multiple participants. In this research, we first explain how to accurately identify and interpret tables. Next, we outline the requirements and procedures of the task1,2,3,4. Additionally, we present the submission outcomes and analyze the submission strategies used by the task's five evaluation teams.5,6,7,8,9

This analysis examines the conceptual underpinnings of quantum mechanics, specifically focusing on its non-local and probabilistic elements. In understanding these principles, the traditional view of numbers takes on a more intricate role. In quantum mechanics, numbers are utilised not just as measurements, but also as fundamental entities. Upon closer inspection, this more sophisticated approach to numbers reveals connections between quantum mechanics and advanced mathematical concepts, including the theory of complicated numbers. In the early 20th century, complicated numbers emerged as a result of efforts to extend complex numbers to a more general framework, facilitating the representation of trigonometric functions through geometric methods similar to those used with complex numbers. In the context of quantum mechanics, complicated numbers offer a potential replacement for complex numbers, enabling a more unified and intuitive handling of the theory's fundamental laws.

This research introduces a modified dimension concept, called r-dimensional dimension, and a corresponding metric dimension variant, called trimmed metric dimension, tailored for finite graphs. We utilize the concept of distance maps to quantify distance parameters in graphs. Specifically, a graph G's trimmed metric dimension is defined as the minimum cardinality of a distinct set of vertices R, which can determine the distance map of every other vertex in G with a relative error rate of at most r/n, where n represents the total number of vertices in G. This idea is built upon Thue's theorem and generalizes the metric dimension concept. We also derive lower bounds for the trimmed metric dimension of various graphs, which improves upon existing lower bounds for the standard dimension in certain graphs. Furthermore, this study offers a polynomial-time algorithm to calculate the trimmed metric dimension for graphs with diameter 2.
These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing horizontal groundwater flow and water table behavior for a class of graduate students.

This study proposes an innovative method for effectively eliminating sulfur dioxide emissions from the output of low-temperature flue gas. The primary goal is to achieve the lowest achievable sulfur dioxide levels in the output air, in accordance with the EU's National Emission Ceiling Directive. To optimize the process, the required amounts of the oxidant ozone were kept minimal, and UV light was used to enhance its interaction with SO$_2$ and increase the overall removal efficiency. The outcomes demonstrate that a combination of ozone and UV light can achieve nearly complete SO$_2$ removal in the flue gas, yielding up to 99.995% destruction rate, solely dependent on the UV irradiation's intensity.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, developers are facing a significant challenge in testing and evaluating the intricate electrical circuits underlying this type of computer system. The vast disparity between computing scales requires testers to possess significant expertise in both circuit design and biological realism. To address this issue, we have created a simulation environment that leverages SystemC to concurrently test various aspects of the system during different design stages. This enables simulations to be run quickly on standard PCs, effectively mitigating the need for extensive hardware-based testing. Furthermore, our framework allows users to swiftly explore and implement multiple simulation scenarios before settling on a suitable configuration.

This research introduces a novel machine learning framework, indeterminacy forests, designed to learn from instances that lack consensus on the outcome, possibly due to noisy data or conflicting assumptions. The model learns to reconcile discrepancies in the training data by incorporating logical constraints and a quantitative uncertainty measure for classification. The latter is calculated using a modular approach, taking into account the likelihood of each instance and the degree of inconsistency. The system can learn from both certain and uncertain knowledge bases, providing a rigorous argumentation framework that's compatible with both classical and intuitionistic logic. The model's performance is evaluated on several datasets, including argumentation schemes, real-world applications, and virtual experiments, demonstrating improved accuracy and adaptability when dealing with uncertain data.

The prunedDTW algorithm excels at efficiently comparing time series, especially when searching for similar patterns. A recent modification, early discarding prunedDTW (EDPD), further enhances performance by optimizing the decision process. Our study evaluates EDPD's potential advantages. Notably, EDPW's suboptimal feature, where its distance calculation might not always be most accurate, can be circumvented by refraining from committing to a decision until a specific point in the algorithm's progression. This 'wait' variant, WDPD, exhibits accelerated decision-making and reduced memory usage while maintaining prunedDTW's suboptimal characteristic. Consequently, both EDPD and WDPD demonstrate speed and memory gains over prunedDTW. Moreover, EDPD surpasses prunedDTW in terms of execution speed and memory consumption. Both methods show potential in time series similarity search tasks.

Current educational tools in software testing often overlook key concepts such as code review, code quality, and process validation. To address this gap, we've developed the Testing Tutor, an intelligent system combining concept-based learning with hands-on testing experience to help students improve code quality and align testing activities with relevant educational objectives. We compared the effects of two testing approaches - extensive and focused - on students' learning outcomes, including their learning experiences, cognitive load, and overall performance. The study revealed both approaches yielded comparable results but highlighted the importance of effective feedback and efficient use of students' time to optimize concept-based learning.

In domains where correctness is critical, such as law, medicine, transportation, and nuclear power, it is indispensable to comprehend which specific factors a model based on deep neural networks (DNN) used to reach a conclusion. Although numerous studies have investigated the interpretability of DNN, it remains an area of considerable research inquiry. This paper offers an innovative approach to bridging the gap between current interpretability methods and the requirements of high-reliability critical systems. By integrating the methodology of concept analysis and using constraints derived from point-wise decision-making data to inform an integer linear programming (ILP) problem, we have developed a framework that identifies understandable patterns in data and maps them to a set of 'concepts.' This framework also enables us to generate explanations for individual predictions through a novel ILP problem. Furthermore, our method inherently includes the inputs used by the DNN during its training, thus ensuring it remains impartial and can be easily verified. Experimental evaluations using various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in identifying meaningful patterns in data and individual predictions. Additionally, explanations generated by our method and evaluations from multiple stakeholders confirm that it is preferred over existing methods.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are widely used for node classification and link prediction in various graph-based applications. While they have shown impressive performance on several benchmarks, our research reveals a concerning issue with GCNs - their tendency to produce overly smoothed features. By applying an extra linear layer as a 'penultimate layer', our experiments demonstrate that GCNs can maintain both improved accuracy and enhanced feature details. Furthermore, we identify the source of the over-blurring effect as the result ofthonic matrix multiplication and the limitations of representational capacity. Based on these findings, we propose the inclusion of a 'penultimate layer' as a crucial component of GCNs to mitigate the negative consequences of the over-blurring effect.

A search for dark matter produced in association with a Z boson that decays into two electrons or two muons, using a LHC proton-proton collision dataset at 13 TeV and with a total luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The dataset was recorded using the CMS detector with a two-electron or two-muon trigger. The search spans a significant range of invariant mass of the dark matter particle from 5 GeV/c$^2$ to 300 GeV/c$^2$. The statistical significance of observed events exceeds that of standard model predictions by 0.4 to 1.4 sigma. The results are consistent with expectations from standard model processes.

We propose several new distribution functions that build on the established $f_{\Delta}$ function, depending on the transverse momentum transfer $k_\perp$, to describe the characteristics of quasi-particles in the JIMWLK equation's linear regime. Additionally, two of these functions have direct correlations with the quasi-particle number and momentum densities of the gluelump states.

Let X be a topological space with Hausdorff properties. This paper's research focuses on the conditions under which the mapping space Map_(R)(X,R) is homogeneous when given a specific topology, specifically when it possesses local compactness and a continuous nature. It is well established that Map_(R)(X,R) is homogeneous when X is a compact Hausdorff space. Building upon previous studies (III), it is demonstrated that Map_(R)(X,R) is homogeneous if X is a Tychonoff space with a certain compact-stocking property. Furthermore, it is shown that for any topological space Y, if Y is homeomorphic to Map_(R)(X,R) for a compact-stocking X, then Y is a topological group.

actively sought after due to the significant advantages it offers in reducing film
thickness and lowering growth temperatures. Nevertheless, achieving remote
epitaxy consistently is challenging, largely due to the alternative possibilities of
pinhole epitaxy and van der Waals epitaxy depending on the film's size and local
conditions. This study investigates the effects of film size and local conditions on

epitaxial process through precise size management.

By using a specific method for modeling, we are able to assess the tendencies in this data under certain conditions and it is also possible to extend the results to include external factors. What's more, our research shows that similar patterns exist in various subsets of the data and it is possible to make accurate predictions about these subsets without significantly changing their characteristics.
